true_answer: The tricky case is this: what if Bob did not get a 90 on the final? Maybe he passes the class, maybe he doesn’t. Did I lie in either case? I think not. In these last two cases, P was false, and the statement P → Q was true. In the first case, Q was true, and so was P → Q . So P → Q is true when either P is false or Q is true. Just to be clear, although we sometimes read P → Q as “ P implies Q ”, we are not insisting that there is some causal relationship between the statements P and Q .
